sources.title: Planning for Secure Water Futures in Contexts of Drought and Displacement: Evidence from Mafraq, Jordan
sources.organization: UN-Habitat Jordan and International Institute for Environment and Development
geographic_coverage: Dahiyyat Al-Malik Abdullah neighborhood, Mafraq City
sources.temporal_coverage: Neighborhood fieldwork and water assessment reported in 2026; selected historical water, population and satellite indicators date to 2014–2025.
sources.methodology: Mixed methods: desk review, GIS, 70-household survey, fieldwork and stakeholder workshops.
sources.limitations: Mafraq case; local survey is not national; over-abstraction is also a water deficit driver.

sources.title: Integrating Climate Security into Policies: Roadmap for Jordan
sources.temporal_coverage: Qualitative risk pathways and institutional assessment, 2023; climate projections discussed in the report extend through 2100.
sources.methodology: Year-long desk research, interviews, consultations and government validation.
sources.limitations: Qualitative pathways synthesize secondary research; no causal impact evaluation.

sources.title: Vulnerability Assessment of the Water Sector to Climate Change in Jordan
sources.organization: United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia
sources.temporal_coverage: Reference climate period 1995–2014; near-term 2021–2040 and mid-term 2041–2060 projections.
sources.methodology: RICCAR geospatial water-sector assessment combines exposure, sensitivity and adaptive-capacity indicators with six downscaled climate models.
sources.limitations: National assessment; some indicators were omitted where comparable data were unavailable; projections are model outputs, not observations.

sources.title: Jordan Country Climate and Development Report
sources.temporal_coverage: Country conditions and regional shocks through 2022; selected climate projections extend to 2040.
sources.methodology: World Bank country climate and development analysis; relevant executive-summary passages inspected.
sources.limitations: National-level findings; inspected executive-summary projection does not specify its climate scenario.

sources.title: Completion of ICRC Water Program: Host Communities and Syrian Refugees in Jordan 2014–2023
sources.organization: International Committee of the Red Cross
sources.temporal_coverage: ICRC infrastructure program 2014–2022; evaluation findings through 2022 and capacity-building actions in 2023.
sources.methodology: Report compiles works and external evaluation through 2022.
sources.limitations: Efficiency later declined amid maintenance gaps.

claims.paraphrase: In Dahiyyat Al-Malik Abdullah, 2022 Amman–Zarqa abstraction was 162.4 MCM versus 87.5 MCM safe yield; the report identifies chronic hydrological drought.
claims.limitations: Over-abstraction is primary; climate attribution is not isolated.

claims.paraphrase: Surveyed households: 27% lacked network connection; summer supply fell and 63% reported inadequate pressure.
71% of Syrian versus 25% of Jordanian households had never applied; barriers included zones, fees and landlord support, while Syrians could not register meters individually.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Report links displacement status with formal water-access barriers.

claims.paraphrase: Unregulated areas cover 62% of the neighborhood; rural zoning prevents Yarmouk Water Company extending services to some households.
GMM's climate-resilient master plan and Urban Observatory support planning; initiatives focus on flood mitigation.
Residents use rooftop storage, conservation, sharing and household adjustments, absorbing service-gap costs.
The roadmap says climate-exacerbated water insecurity may intensify disputes and anti-refugee sentiment, eroding social cohesion.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Authors connect climate-water stress with disputes and anti-refugee sentiment.

claims.paraphrase: Reduced rainfall and drought could harm rural livelihoods, spur movement to Amman and raise competition for strained services.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Authors link climate-related rural stress with migration, competition and possible community conflict.

claims.paraphrase: Climate-related water scarcity could undermine tribal water agreements, especially in livestock-producing areas.
claims.limitations: No local agreement or incident evaluated.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Authors say water scarcity may weaken tribal water governance.

claims.paraphrase: In 2023, climate-security policy integration remained inadequate due to awareness, technical-capacity and funding limits.
At 1995–2014 baseline, desert areas had over 80 April–September hot days; SSP5-8.5 projects about 40% of summer days near-term and 50% mid-term above 35°C.
claims.scenario: SSP5-8.5; six downscaled models; 2021–2040 and 2041–2060 versus 1995–2014.
claims.limitations: These are modeled climate-zone results, not observed future outcomes or administrative-area estimates.

claims.paraphrase: Under SSP5-8.5, modeled drought frequency generally rises across Jordan by mid-term; the report identifies Amman and areas south of the city as future flood-risk locations.
claims.limitations: The report notes spatial and model uncertainty; the flood-risk pathway is linked to dry soils and runoff.

claims.locator: Executive summary, PDF p. 9 (printed p. IV).
claims.paraphrase: The 2022 CCDR reports 97 m³ of water per person annually and projects climate change could reduce per-capita availability about 30% by 2040 while raising demand.
claims.scenario: The inspected executive-summary passage does not specify a climate scenario.
claims.limitations: National-level CCDR projection; executive-summary passage omits scenario and uncertainty range.

claims.locator: Executive summary, PDF p. 9 (printed p. IV).
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR says regional conflicts since 2011 led to an influx of 1.3 million Syrian refugees; population growth increased pressure on service delivery and scarce water and land.
claims.limitations: The 1.3 million figure and service-pressure framing are report-era national context, not a current refugee count.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The CCDR links regional conflict to Syrian refugee influx and increased pressure on resources and services.

claims.paraphrase: Conflict-driven Syrian refugee arrivals strained water systems in Irbid and Mafraq; remote infrastructure was aged.
institutions: International Committee of the Red Cross
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: ICRC says conflict-related arrivals strained northern host-area water systems.

claims.paraphrase: Efficiency rose from 20% to 86% after works, then fell to 65% in 2022 amid maintenance, spare-parts and staffing gaps.
institutions: International Committee of the Red Cross

claims.paraphrase: Supply rose from 32 to 107 litres per capita daily, then 85 in 2022; people below 20 litres fell from 26,000 to 6,000.
affected_groups: people with very low water access
institutions: International Committee of the Red Cross

claims.paraphrase: In 2023 ICRC developed a training centre in Hofa, Irbid, and trained 40 operators from four northern governorates in maintenance.
institutions: International Committee of the Red Cross

gaps: The IWMI 2024 Irbid–Ramtha vulnerability report was located, but its official item page returned HTTP 429 and the original report was not inspected; search metadata was not used as evidence.

The reviewed climate-security roadmap is a 2023 qualitative national synthesis; no current 2026 local study was found verifying its prospective climate–security pathways in specific Jordanian districts.
The UN-Habitat Mafraq survey is limited to 70 households in one neighborhood; its differences should not be generalized to all refugee-hosting communities.
No inspected primary passage established that water scarcity caused conflict; climate-security links are recorded only as conditional pathways explicitly stated by Adelphi.
